tagVocabulary.AI-assisted: Built primarily through AI-assisted development (Claude Code), with architecture, direction and review by me.
tagVocabulary.from-scratch: Written by hand, line by line, without AI assistance.
tagVocabulary.conceptual-experiment: Built to test an idea rather than to ship. The result is the finding, not the product.

projects.title: ZEO 2.0
projects.tagline: A personal agentic OS as a native Rust desktop app.
projects.summary: The most technically ambitious project in the archive. Kimi K2 drives reasoning through a config-swappable backend that also speaks Groq, local llama.cpp and Ollama DeepSeek-R1. Built as a Cargo workspace: zeo-model handles SSE streaming over an OpenAI-compatible layer, zeo-vault does safe Obsidian file operations, plus a gstack skill runner, a hardware scheduler, a RAG semantic index and knowledge-graph extraction. The UI is a paged command deck with a real shell terminal and a force-directed graph. Phases 1-3 plus a second wave shipped, including blue-green dual-instance deploys with automatic rollback.
projects.timeline: Built Jul 2026 · archived to GitHub Aug 2026
projects.how: I structured it as a Cargo workspace with clear module boundaries (zeo-model for SSE streaming, zeo-vault for safe file ops) so the model backend stays swappable without touching the UI. I built it phase by phase, testing each layer before the next, then shipped blue-green dual-instance deploys with automatic rollback so a bad build can never take the whole thing down. The hard-won lesson was keeping the streaming, the shell and the graph in sync — that forced me to actually understand the event flow rather than just wiring calls together.

projects.title: ZEO Interface (v1)
projects.tagline: First cut of ZEO: a Tauri front end over a Rust core with a Claude Agent SDK sidecar.
projects.summary: Notable for two things it got right early: a live vault indexer that scanned a real Zettelkasten and rendered actual topology instead of mock data, and a UI-command channel that let the agent open windows and post notifications rather than only printing chat. Also carries the ZEO persona brief - a scoped assistant that never operates outside its home folder and moves files to .trash/ instead of deleting them.
projects.how: This was the first cut, and I concentrated on two things I knew would matter: a live vault indexer that scanned a real Zettelkasten and rendered actual topology instead of mock data, and a UI-command channel so the agent could open windows and post notifications rather than only print chat. Building against real data early exposed problems mock data hid. I also wrote the ZEO persona brief — scoping the agent to its home folder and .trash/ instead of deleting — which taught me how much of agent safety is just careful constraints.

projects.title: Minerva & Hermes
projects.tagline: An always-on personal agent reachable from WhatsApp that delegates coding to Claude Code.
projects.summary: Minerva acts as the CEO - persistent memory, schedules, file management on the Mac, mentor mode - and delegates all coding into Claude Code with ruflo swarms. The split is deliberately economic: chat and orchestration run on a free model, and heavy work is routed where the Pro subscription already pays for it.
projects.how: I wanted an always-on assistant reachable from WhatsApp. I split the architecture deliberately for cost: chat and orchestration run on a free model, while heavy coding is delegated to Claude Code through ruflo swarms. Wiring it up meant learning how the Hermes gateway routes messages and where state lives, so a phone conversation survives even while a delegated build runs for minutes.

projects.title: KARIN
projects.tagline: An AI software delivery team: intake, plan, build, review.
projects.summary: You describe an app in chat; KARIN turns it into a requirements brief, a project-manager agent writes the plan and delegates, backend and frontend agents build their slices, and a QA agent checks the result against the original brief. Every agent updates its lane in project-status.json and a live dashboard shows who is doing what. Generalised out of the Simmer build.
projects.how: I generalised this out of the Simmer build after watching a multi-agent workflow run. The design: intake turns a description into a requirements brief, a PM agent plans and delegates, backend and frontend agents build their slices, and a QA agent checks the result against the brief — every agent updates project-status.json so a live dashboard shows who is doing what. Building it forced me to design the contracts between agents carefully, because ambiguity anywhere becomes a deadlock.

projects.title: CLARA
projects.tagline: A self-extending assistant that retrieves past solutions instead of regenerating them.
projects.summary: Solved problems are embedded with nomic-embed-text and stored in a local on-disk Qdrant collection, so a similar question retrieves and adapts a past solution instead of regenerating from scratch. An analyzer classifies the domain, an extension builder writes and executes Python, and an Obsidian connector files results into a vault organised by subject. Fully local, and the only prototype here with a real test suite.
projects.timeline: Built May 2026 · archived to GitHub Aug 2026
projects.how: I built the retrieval loop first: solved problems get embedded with nomic-embed-text and stored in a local Qdrant collection, so a similar question retrieves and adapts a past solution instead of regenerating from scratch. Then I layered the analyzer (domain classification), the extension builder (writes and runs Python) and an Obsidian connector. It's the only prototype here with a real pytest suite — I wanted tests because retrieval behaviour is exactly the kind of thing that breaks silently.

projects.title: Neonate — The Learning Agent
projects.tagline: An LLM plays God generating world events; a newborn neural net learns from prediction error.
projects.summary: The most original idea in the archive. An LLM reads world state and generates the next event; a newborn neural-net agent receives that as sensory input, acts, and updates its weights from prediction error. Everything is logged step by step and watched through a live monitor page. Bolted on around it: a voice retraining script, an English-teacher module and a memory store.
projects.timeline: Built May 2026 · archived to GitHub Aug 2026
projects.how: The concept: an LLM reads world state and generates the next event; a tiny neural-net agent receives that as sensory input, acts, and updates its weights from prediction error. I wrote the agent's forward and backward pass by hand rather than leaning on a framework, because the whole point was to watch it learn. Everything is logged step-by-step and viewed through a live monitor page, so I could see exactly where the learning curve happened — and where it stalled.

projects.title: Minerva Workspace
projects.tagline: A claude-flow workspace scaffold with MCP config.
projects.summary: Set up with a project brief and MCP configuration, never grown into a working system. Archived for completeness.
projects.how: A claude-flow workspace scaffold with MCP config. I set it up with a project brief and MCP configuration to test the workflow shape, but never grew it into a working system. Even the scaffold taught me what a minimal agent workspace needs: a brief, a memory location and a way to call tools.

projects.title: PokerApp
projects.tagline: Multiplayer Texas hold'em: native iOS SwiftUI client against a Node/TypeScript backend.
projects.summary: Built across five deliberate phases: data model, auth and a chip economy on Prisma and Postgres; a poker engine core wrapping poker-ts with seven test suites; a real-time layer using WebSocket transport with Redis pub/sub relaying per-table state, turn timers and disconnect handling; then the SwiftUI client with a glassmorphism table that changes its landmark theming by country. The engineering high point was a removePlayer() deadlock found in live play, fixed, then proven necessary by disabling the guard to reproduce the bug and re-enabling it, with an independent agent re-verifying all seven checkpoints.
projects.timeline: Built Jul-Aug 2026 · archived to GitHub Aug 2026
projects.how: I built it in five deliberate phases so each layer was testable before the next: data model, auth and a chip economy on Prisma/Postgres; the poker engine wrapping poker-ts with seven test suites; the real-time layer (WebSocket + Redis pub/sub for table state, turn timers and disconnect handling); then the SwiftUI client. The high point was a removePlayer() deadlock found in live play — I fixed it, then disabled the guard to reproduce the bug and re-enabled it to prove the fix was necessary, and had an independent agent re-verify all seven checkpoints.

projects.title: Tally
projects.tagline: A rules-based job-application tracker for London graduate accountancy schemes.
projects.summary: Pulls real roles from live job APIs and ATS endpoints - Pinpoint, The Muse, Workday tenant probing - parses an uploaded CV to auto-fill the profile, scores each role against it, drafts applications, tracks status and reads reply mail. Front end is vanilla JS and CSS with no framework and no build step, falling back to seed data when the backend is down. The README makes a point of it: no AI anywhere, every rule explicit and inspectable. The most finished project in the archive.
projects.timeline: Built Aug 2026 · archived to GitHub Aug 2026
projects.how: The constraint was explicit: no AI anywhere, every rule inspectable. I pulled real roles from live job APIs and ATS endpoints (Pinpoint, The Muse, Workday tenant probing), parsed an uploaded CV to auto-fill the profile, scored each role against it and tracked status. The front end is vanilla JS with no build step. Writing the scoring rules by hand forced me to make them precise — a fuzzy 'good fit' doesn't compile.

projects.title: Simmer
projects.tagline: Mobile companion for a weekly meal subscription.
projects.summary: A countdown to the Tuesday 1pm order lock-in, order history with one-tap reorder, and mobile plan management. FastAPI with SQLAlchemy, Alembic and JWT on Postgres behind a React Native and Expo front end. Built through a multi-agent Claude Code workflow with its own live build-progress dashboard - the run that later became KARIN.
projects.how: This was the run that later became KARIN. I built a FastAPI backend with SQLAlchemy, Alembic and JWT on Postgres behind a React Native/Expo front end, orchestrated through a multi-agent Claude Code workflow with its own live build-progress dashboard. The real learning was watching the workflow itself: where the pipeline saved time, and where it still needed a human to catch it.

projects.title: Portfolio Site
projects.tagline: Dark single-page portfolio on React 19 with GSAP scroll animation.
projects.summary: All content driven from one config file. Its own project thumbnails are a useful index of earlier work: ASL recognition, blackjack, a calculator, a family tree, smart glasses and space debris. This is the site the archive is intended to feed.
projects.how: This very site. The frontend was AI-assisted, but the planning wasn't: section structure, the three-tag taxonomy and all the content came first, and the projects feed means updating the site is editing one JSON file. It's the meta-project that ties the archive together.

projects.title: Content Creation Automation
projects.tagline: End-to-end pipeline for a dark cinematic storytelling brand on TikTok and Reels.
projects.summary: Generate frames, animate them image-to-video with Kling, narrate with ElevenLabs, detect beats, burn in word-level captions and assemble the final cut. Five finished stories were produced in May, alongside a brand strategy document whose central finding shaped the plan: Instagram suppresses pure AI content, so TikTok became the primary channel. Generated output (rendered frames, narration audio, finished videos and per-account assets) is excluded from the archive; the pipeline that produces them is here.
projects.how: I built the pipeline in stages: generate frames, animate image-to-video with Kling, narrate with ElevenLabs, detect beats, burn word-level captions and assemble the final cut. Five stories were produced in May, and a brand-strategy doc changed the plan — Instagram suppresses pure AI content, so TikTok became the primary channel. The lesson: the tooling matters less than knowing where the platform will actually distribute it.

projects.title: Dual-Engine Crime Forecasting
projects.tagline: Weekly crime-risk prediction across Greater London, fusing XGBoost with a local LLM reading the news.
projects.summary: COMP1682, and by session count the most worked-on project here. Two engines run in parallel: a quantitative one training XGBoost on UK Police data aggregated to H3 resolution-8 hexagons with lag features and a time-held-out split, reported on MAE, RMSE and PAI@10%; and a contextual one where a local Ollama model reads BBC London and Guardian coverage, extracts macro events (protests, fixtures, weather, transport disruption) and turns them into per-area risk modifiers. The two are fused multiplicatively, and each hexagon carries a confidence rating based on whether the engines agree.
projects.timeline: Built Jul-Aug 2026 · archived to GitHub Aug 2026
projects.how: Two engines in parallel. Quantitative: XGBoost on UK Police data aggregated to H3 resolution-8 hexagons, with lag features and a time-held-out split, reported on MAE, RMSE and PAI@10%. Contextual: a local Ollama model reads BBC London and Guardian coverage, extracts macro events and turns them into per-area risk modifiers. I fused them multiplicatively and gave each hexagon a confidence rating based on whether the engines agree. Holding out time — not random rows — was the lesson that mattered most for a forecast that's supposed to predict the future.

projects.title: IDEA 49 — Commodities Signal Engine
projects.tagline: Adaptive quant models plus news sentiment across gold, oil and silver.
projects.summary: An adaptive quant engine trains on a two-year window with per-asset persisted models, a news engine pulls live headlines into a macro vector with a confidence score and per-asset sentiment, and a decision layer blends the two at a deliberately cautious 5% news weight. A parallel R sub-project runs regression modelling on the same gold series.
projects.how: An adaptive quant engine trains on a two-year window with per-asset persisted models; a news engine pulls live headlines into a macro vector with a confidence score and per-asset sentiment; a decision layer blends them at a deliberately cautious 5% news weight. I ran a parallel R sub-project doing regression on the same gold series. It was abandoned after one session, and that's the honest finding: the signal wasn't there yet, and knowing when to stop is part of the work.

projects.title: Qwen Launcher Kit
projects.tagline: Five double-clickable launchers for running Qwen3.5-9B locally five different ways.
projects.summary: Ollama in fast mode with thinking disabled, Ollama with thinking on, MLX interactive chat, an MLX OpenAI-compatible server on port 8080, and Open WebUI on 3000. The Web UI script does the real work: sets the Ollama base URL, disables telemetry and auth, persists a one-hour keep-alive and a 16k context through launchctl, polls the port until healthy, then opens the browser.
projects.how: Five double-clickable launchers for running Qwen3.5-9B locally five different ways. The Web UI script does the real work: sets the Ollama base URL, disables telemetry and auth, persists a one-hour keep-alive and a 16k context through launchctl, polls the port until healthy, then opens the browser. Writing these meant actually reading the launchctl and port-polling behaviour instead of pasting commands.

projects.title: Blackjack GUI
projects.tagline: Tkinter blackjack with a full side-bet layer.
projects.summary: Pair detection, a three-card-poker payout table covering three-of-a-kind, straight, flush and pair-plus-kicker, and a dealer top-three simulation. Roughly 250 lines, still carrying the filename VS Code gave it. This is the game behind the portfolio's blackjack thumbnail.
projects.how: Tkinter blackjack with a side-bet layer: pair detection, a three-card-poker payout table (three-of-a-kind, straight, flush, pair-plus-kicker) and a dealer top-three simulation — about 250 lines. Writing the payout logic by hand is exactly the kind of detail work that catches you out if you don't actually understand the rules.

projects.title: Early Web Experiments
projects.tagline: The oldest code in the archive: a colour-blindness game and a small blog.
projects.summary: All plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no tooling. A colour-blindness game with a practice mode and background music, and ghost post - a small blog with post, read and about pages and a hand-drawn logo, kept in three parallel revisions. Where it started.
projects.how: Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no tooling: a colour-blindness game with a practice mode and background music, and a small blog with a hand-drawn logo. This is where I started, and building without frameworks is why the fundamentals stuck — I had to understand the DOM itself, not the abstraction.

projects.title: ASL Sign Recognition
projects.tagline: A trained CNN for American Sign Language recognition.
projects.summary: Model and label weights alongside a hand-sign dataset and a recognition script. This is the ASL entry on the portfolio. Trained weights (.pth) are excluded as binaries, but the labelled hand-sign dataset is included so the model can be retrained from the included script.
projects.how: I trained a CNN for ASL recognition: collected a labelled hand-sign dataset, trained the model and kept the weights and labels together so it can be retrained from the included script. Working with a real image dataset meant learning the data pipeline — cleaning, splitting, and why a model behaves differently on live video than on test frames.

projects.title: Hand Particles
projects.tagline: A MediaPipe hand-tracking particle toy.
projects.summary: Real-time hand skeleton tracking driven by a landmark model, pushed into a particle field.
projects.how: A MediaPipe hand-tracking toy: real-time hand skeleton from a landmark model, pushed into a particle field. It's small, but it forced me to understand the landmark model's output format and the coordinate mapping into screen space.

projects.title: Campus Services Booking System
projects.tagline: Java OO domain model for booking campus study rooms and services.
projects.summary: A full object-oriented domain model with users, staff and student directories, study rooms, services, bookings, booking status and a booking manager. Paired with a Maven-built Secure Access-Control System covered by JUnit tests.
projects.how: A full object-oriented domain model in Java — users, staff and student directories, study rooms, services, bookings, booking status and a booking manager — paired with a Maven-built Secure Access-Control System covered by JUnit tests. Modelling the domain before writing code was the lesson: get the object graph right and the rest follows.

projects.title: Boolean Expression Compiler
projects.tagline: A boolean calculator built with lex and yacc.
projects.summary: A generated scanner and parser plus a hand-written driver, implementing a boolean expression calculator end to end. Submitted alongside a six-task logbook.
projects.how: A boolean expression calculator built with lex and yacc: a generated scanner and parser plus a hand-written driver, submitted with a six-task logbook. Writing the grammar and watching the parser build the tree made compilers concrete in a way reading about them never did.

projects.title: LSTM Stock Forecast
projects.tagline: Five-day AAPL closing-price forecast from a 60-day lookback window.
projects.summary: Group 12 coursework. Downloads AAPL data with yfinance, trains an LSTM over a 60-day lookback window and predicts the next five closing prices at once. Adapted from published examples with sources cited in the file header.
projects.how: Group coursework: download AAPL data with yfinance, train an LSTM over a 60-day lookback window and predict the next five closing prices. Adapted from published examples with sources cited. The real learning was understanding why the lookback window and the one-shot-five-days output shape the problem so much.

projects.title: Asteroid Diameter Regression
projects.tagline: Predicting near-Earth object diameter for planetary defence risk.
projects.summary: Regression modelling on near-Earth object data to estimate asteroid diameter as a planetary-defence risk indicator, submitted as the second of two courseworks for the module.
projects.how: Regression modelling on near-Earth object data to estimate asteroid diameter as a planetary-defence risk indicator. This was about feature selection and diagnostics more than the model — understanding which variables actually drive diameter and checking the residuals told me whether the model was any good.

projects.title: Algorithms & Data Structures
projects.tagline: CLRS-based implementations across two years of study.
projects.summary: A chained hash table built from scratch against the CLRS chapter structure and exercised through a demo harness, plus linked-list and binary-search lab work. The year 1 half holds four-person group coursework with two solutions and an optimised variant.
projects.how: CLRS-based implementations across two years: a chained hash table built from scratch against the chapter structure, plus linked-list and binary-search labs and four-person group coursework. Implementing the structures by hand is why I can reason about their costs instead of trusting a library.

projects.title: Statistical Techniques with R
projects.tagline: A seeded statistical analysis where every submission differs by student ID.
projects.summary: The analysis is seeded from the student ID so no two submissions share a dataset. Worked through practice scripts and drafts to a final report.
projects.how: A statistical analysis seeded from my student ID so no two submissions share a dataset, worked through practice scripts and drafts to a final report. The discipline was in the process — hypothesis, model, diagnostics, repeat — rather than any single line of code.

projects.title: University Coursework Archive
projects.tagline: Remaining Greenwich CS modules: labs, reports and early Python.
projects.summary: The remaining assessed modules: first-year Python (timetable generator, quiz, calculator, Fibonacci, line graphs, the original blackjack), a paired Scheme project with Tkinter GUI labs, software engineering with an ERD design, Unix and Linux lab work, and the Operating Systems and Information Security courseworks. Reports in .docx and .pdf are excluded as binaries; the code and lab work is here.
projects.how: The remaining assessed modules: first-year Python (timetable generator, quiz, calculator, the original blackjack), a Scheme project with Tkinter labs, software-engineering ERD design, Unix/Linux labs, and the OS and security courseworks. The breadth is the point — each module taught a different way of thinking.

projects.title: Galaxy Book → Fedora LLM Box
projects.tagline: Repurposing an unused laptop as a dedicated local-LLM machine.
projects.summary: A plan to repurpose an unused touchscreen Galaxy Book3 (i5-1340P, 8GB RAM, 238GB, Iris Xe) as a dedicated Fedora Workstation machine running Ollama with the Alpaca front end, with the SD slot as the storage escape hatch. Hardware assessed, OS chosen, a full step-by-step install guide written. Execution stopped when the USB drive for the install media turned out to be unusable.
projects.how: A plan to repurpose an unused Galaxy Book3 as a dedicated Fedora + Ollama machine, with the SD slot as the storage escape hatch. I assessed the hardware, chose the OS and wrote a full step-by-step install guide — then execution stalled when the USB install media turned out unusable. I'm keeping it here because planning and hardware reality are different skills.
